title: BluePeak x Redwood — Dedicated Tier Plus POC scoping (throughput floor + burst + reporting)
next_steps: Redwood to send Tier Plus POC packet: proposed shape(s) in us-west-2, preliminary throughput floor numbers, and burst policy summary.
BluePeak to share 2–3 representative prompts (short + long context) and target model(s)/versions for benchmarking.
Schedule a 45-min technical kickoff to set up observability access (Console views + metrics export) and agree on measurement window.
Redwood to confirm whether cross-AZ HA is in-scope for Tier Plus POC or deferred to Premium discussion.
BluePeak to confirm preferred region (us-west vs us-east) and data retention requirements for logs/traces.
action_items: Stephanie Nguyen: Send POC scoping email w/ proposed Tier Plus entitlements + commercial guardrails by 2025-04-03.
Simran Kaur: Draft success criteria table (throughput floor, p95 latency, burst behavior) and share benchmark plan by 2025-04-04.
Hyejin Park: Validate available Dedicated shapes in us-west and expected lead time; reply in thread by 2025-04-03.
Jordan Lee (BluePeak): Provide workload details (avg input/output tokens, concurrency pattern, streaming vs non-streaming) by 2025-04-04.
Priya Nair (BluePeak): Share target model/version constraints + eval prompts by 2025-04-04.
topics: What BluePeak considers “success” for Dedicated Tier Plus
Throughput floor definition (tokens/sec) and how it’s measured
Burst policy: what counts as burst, duration limits, and metering
Model/version pinning and how variability affects commitments
Observability: dashboards, exports, and who can access what
Exclusions and edge cases (client throttling, retries, warmup, streaming accounting)
summary: POC scoping call to align on Dedicated Tier Plus success criteria for BluePeak. The team discussed Redwood’s throughput-floor approach (tokens/sec measured over a rolling window, pinned model/version, excluding customer-side throttling and certain client-driven errors), plus how “burst” capacity works (short-term above-commit usage when headroom exists, separately metered). BluePeak emphasized needing a clear floor they can plan around for a customer-facing feature launch, plus enough reporting to prove compliance internally (SRE dashboards + export). Redwood will propose one or two standard shapes in us-west, run a benchmark with BluePeak prompts, and define the POC measurement plan (window, traffic generator, and acceptance thresholds).

Fireflies.ai — Transcript

Title: BluePeak x Redwood — Dedicated Tier Plus POC scoping (throughput floor + burst + reporting)
Date: 2025-04-02
Time: 10:00 AM PT
Duration: 52 min
Attendees (Redwood): Stephanie Nguyen, Simran Kaur, Hyejin Park
Attendees (BluePeak): Jordan Lee, Priya Nair, Sam Ortega, Maya Chen (joined late)

Auto-generated notes (may be incomplete)
- Summary: Discussed Tier Plus POC scope, throughput floor measurement, burst behavior, and observability/reporting requirements.
- Action items: Redwood to send POC packet and benchmark plan; BluePeak to share prompts + workload details.


[00:00] Stephanie Nguyen: Hey everyone, can you hear me okay?
[00:02] Jordan Lee: Yep, loud and clear.
[00:03] Priya Nair: Yeah.
[00:04] Simran Kaur: I can hear you.
[00:05] Hyejin Park: Same.

[00:10] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. Thanks for making time. Goal today is basically to scope the POC for Dedicated Tier Plus—what success looks like, what we’re measuring for throughput floor and burst, and what reporting you need to feel good. Then we can send a written plan.

[00:27] Jordan Lee: Great. Just to level set, we’re trying to move off a patchwork of endpoints. We have some traffic on Bedrock and some on a vendor API. The big pain is we can’t predict throughput and then internal folks ask, “are we getting what we pay for,” right.

[00:44] Stephanie Nguyen: Makes sense.

[00:45] Jordan Lee: For Dedicated, we need a floor, not a best effort. And we need to know what happens when we burst. Like, if a launch hits, do we get throttled? Or do we pay extra? Or both.

[01:01] Simran Kaur: Yep, that’s exactly what Tier Plus is intended to address. Can I ask, what’s the workload shape—like chat, batch summarization, embeddings?

[01:11] Priya Nair: Mostly chat. It’s customer support automation. Streaming responses, tool calling sometimes. Context can be… usually 2 to 6k tokens in, output maybe 300 to 800. But we do have long tail, like 20k context on escalations.

[01:32] Simran Kaur: Okay. And model preference? Are you pinned to a specific open model or flexible?

[01:37] Priya Nair: We’re leaning Llama 3.1 70B class. But we’re evaluating a couple. The problem is if you say the floor is X but then the model changes, the floor moves.

[01:49] Stephanie Nguyen: Right. For Dedicated commitments, we typically tie the floor to a specific model + version, and a deployment config. Otherwise it’s impossible to keep it non-gameable.

[02:00] Jordan Lee: That’s fine. We can pin for the POC. Internally we need to see it in writing, at least for the real contract. For POC, we need a clear acceptance criteria.

[02:12] Simran Kaur: Let’s define those. Usually we do something like: “Committed throughput floor of Y tokens/sec sustained over a rolling measurement window,” plus constraints: max context, streaming on/off, and concurrency assumptions.

[02:27] Sam Ortega: Sorry, when you say tokens/sec, is that output tokens only or input + output?

[02:33] Simran Kaur: Good question. Our canonical metric is total tokens—input + output—processed by the deployment, but we break it out too. For the floor, we use total tokens/sec because it reflects actual GPU work more consistently.

[02:47] Sam Ortega: And how do you count streaming? We’ve had issues where vendors count partial chunks weirdly.

[02:53] Simran Kaur: Yeah. We count actual generated tokens server-side, not SSE chunk count. There was a bug a while back with double counting in streaming in some systems—ours is fixed and we can show you how it’s instrumented. For POC, we can validate that your numbers match ours by exporting the same counters.

[03:13] Jordan Lee: That’s important. We got burned by “the dashboard says it’s fine” while our app says otherwise.

[03:18] Stephanie Nguyen: Understood. For reporting, Tier Plus includes access to the Dedicated deployment dashboard in Console with throughput floor tracking, and we can also do a daily export (CSV or API) of tokens, errors, and saturation signals.

[03:34] Priya Nair: What’s the measurement window? Like, if we have a five minute dip is that an SLO breach?

[03:40] Hyejin Park: Usually it’s measured over a window like 30 minutes, sometimes 60. The point is to avoid counting short warmups or brief blips as a miss.

[03:49] Simran Kaur: Yeah. And on top of that, internally we do burn-rate alerting. But for POC acceptance we can pick a simpler statement: e.g., “For a sustained load test of N minutes, the average throughput is at least Y and p95 latency is under Z.”

[04:07] Jordan Lee: Okay. Our preference is a load test that looks like production. We can replay traffic or run a generator.

[04:14] Sam Ortega: If we replay, do you guys have IP allow lists? We’re in AWS.

[04:17] Hyejin Park: Yep, for Dedicated we can set allowlists, or we can do a VPC peering option later. For POC we can keep it simpler with public ingress + auth, but we can lock it down.

[04:31] Stephanie Nguyen: Maybe pause on networking—today we’re focusing on throughput and tier entitlements, but we’ll capture security needs.

[04:38] Jordan Lee: Sure.

[04:40] Simran Kaur: On burst: can you describe your burst pattern? Is it “we go from 50 RPS to 200 RPS for an hour,” or more spiky?

[04:49] Priya Nair: Spiky. Product launches, or a customer incident. Could be 3x for like 10 to 20 minutes.

[04:57] Jordan Lee: And sometimes it’s like, the first 3 minutes are insane.

[05:02] Simran Kaur: Got it. Tier Plus generally includes a burst policy where you can exceed the committed floor when there’s headroom in the pool. We meter burst separately so billing can reflect it, but for POC we might just track it. The key thing: burst is not guaranteed in the same way the floor is, but it’s “supported”—we won’t immediately clamp you at the floor.

[05:25] Sam Ortega: So, what happens if there’s no headroom? Do you queue? Do you 429?

[05:31] Hyejin Park: Depends on the deployment’s admission control config. Typically we do bounded queueing to protect latency, then shed with a retry-able status once the queue is full. For Tier Plus, the queue limits are tuned to allow short spikes without tail latency exploding.

[05:49] Jordan Lee: That’s okay as long as we can predict it and see it.

[05:53] Priya Nair: Also, we have a lot of parallel tool calls. If you queue, the tools chain stalls and it cascades.

[06:00] Simran Kaur: Understood. For the POC, we can measure not just throughput but also p95 end-to-end latency and “time to first token” if streaming. We can also set max concurrency guidance so you don’t accidentally overload it and then it looks like we missed the floor.

[06:19] Jordan Lee: Yeah, define “you overloaded it” precisely. That’s always the argument.

[06:24] Stephanie Nguyen: Totally fair. In the dedicated contract language, exclusions usually include customer-side throttling/misuse, like sending above agreed concurrency limits or unsupported context lengths. For POC we can be explicit: we’ll agree on a traffic profile, and we’ll measure against that.

[06:42] Sam Ortega: How do you detect customer-side throttling?

[06:45] Simran Kaur: A couple ways. If your client is doing retries that inflate request rate, we see that. If there’s a high rate of canceled requests or timeouts on the client side, we can tag those. But the simplest is: we look at server-side accepted requests and tokens processed. The SLO is based on what the deployment accepted and processed, not what was attempted and rejected by your own client.

[07:12] Priya Nair: Okay.

[07:14] Jordan Lee: Can we talk about the “floor” unit. Like, do you give us a number, say “80k tokens/sec,” and that’s guaranteed always?

[07:24] Stephanie Nguyen: For the actual tier, it’s a committed floor tied to your shape and model. Always is a strong word; it’s under the conditions we specify—model pinned, within max context, within agreed usage profile. If we miss it due to Redwood causes, there’s a remedy path.

[07:43] Jordan Lee: Remedy meaning credits.

[07:45] Stephanie Nguyen: Typically, yes, service credits. For POC we won’t do credits, but we’ll treat misses as POC failures and we’ll investigate.

[07:55] Sam Ortega: What about failover? Like if a node dies.

[07:58] Hyejin Park: Tier Plus usually has improved failover posture versus Standard, but it’s not full HA like Premium. In practice, for the dedicated pool we can keep a warm spare depending on region and shape availability. For POC, we can decide whether to include a warm spare as part of the test.

[08:18] Jordan Lee: That might be a dealbreaker later, but for now we can focus on steady-state throughput.

[08:25] Simran Kaur: Cool. Let’s define POC success criteria as three buckets: (1) throughput floor in a controlled test, (2) latency targets in that same test, (3) visibility/reporting.

[08:37] Priya Nair: Agree.

[08:38] Simran Kaur: For throughput: can you share target RPS and tokens? If you don’t have exact, we can start with what you need the floor to be.

[08:46] Priya Nair: For launch, we need to sustain around 120 concurrent chats at peak. Each chat is multiple turns. It’s messy.

[08:55] Jordan Lee: Translate: we think around 90 to 120 requests per second at peak, but it depends on prompt size.

[09:03] Simran Kaur: That’s helpful. Another way: what’s your monthly token volume and peak-to-average ratio.

[09:09] Jordan Lee: Peak-to-average is like 4 to 6.

[09:13] Priya Nair: Monthly tokens… I’d rather not say exact, but it’s in the tens of billions.

[09:20] Stephanie Nguyen: That’s enough for now. For POC we can choose a representative slice.

[09:25] Sam Ortega: I care about p95. We get yelled at for p99 but realistically we can accept some tail if it’s controlled.

[09:33] Simran Kaur: What’s your p95 target today?

[09:36] Sam Ortega: Under 2.5 seconds to first token, and under 12 seconds total for typical responses.

[09:43] Priya Nair: That’s for the common case, not the 20k context outliers.

[09:48] Simran Kaur: Perfect. We’ll define common case with a context cap—like 8k or 12k—for the POC acceptance test, and then separately test long context as “best effort / observed.”

[10:03] Jordan Lee: Yeah, we can do that.

[10:05] Stephanie Nguyen: Region preference—still us-west?

[10:08] Jordan Lee: Yes, us-west. Our core infra is in Oregon.

[10:12] Hyejin Park: Great. That constrains available shapes slightly, but we have good coverage.

[10:18] Priya Nair: What shapes are we talking about? Like H100s?

[10:21] Hyejin Park: It depends. Tier Plus usually maps to a standard shape catalog. In us-west we can propose either an A100-based 8 GPU node or an H100-based 8 GPU node, depending on lead time. H100s are tighter supply.

[10:39] Jordan Lee: Lead time matters. We want POC in April.

[10:43] Hyejin Park: For April, A100 is more realistic. H100 might be possible but I need to confirm with fleet.

[10:49] Stephanie Nguyen: We’ll follow up in email with what’s actually available.

[10:53] Simran Kaur: On observability: what do you need access-wise? SRE dashboards? Raw metrics?

[10:59] Sam Ortega: We need both. Ideally we can scrape Prometheus, but I assume you won’t expose that.

[11:05] Simran Kaur: Not direct scraping. But we can provide an API export and we have Grafana-style dashboards in Console. We can also integrate with your Datadog via a metrics forwarder in some cases.

[11:16] Jordan Lee: We’re on Datadog.

[11:18] Sam Ortega: We’d need at minimum: tokens/sec, queue depth, 429 rate, GPU utilization, and latency breakdown.

[11:26] Simran Kaur: Yep. We can share: accepted tokens/sec, request rate, latency percentiles, saturation signals (queue, batcher pressure), and error taxonomy. GPU utilization we expose as a normalized “engine saturation” rather than raw nvidia-smi.

[11:44] Sam Ortega: That’s fine.

[11:46] Priya Nair: Also need model version in the metrics. If someone flips it, we want to know.

[11:51] Simran Kaur: 100%. Model + version tags.

[11:54] Stephanie Nguyen: And Tier Plus includes a monthly report. For POC we can do weekly check-ins with a shared dashboard.

[12:03] Jordan Lee: Weekly check-in works.

[12:05] Priya Nair: Can we talk about evaluation. Like quality regressions? Maybe out of scope.

[12:10] Simran Kaur: For this POC, we can keep it to performance and reliability. But if you have a small eval set, we can run it to ensure quantization or batching changes don’t break your outputs.

[12:22] Priya Nair: Okay.

[12:24] Jordan Lee: Back to burst. If burst is metered, do we get billed extra during POC?

[12:29] Stephanie Nguyen: For POC we can do it as a flat pilot fee or credits, depending on how we structure it. But the important thing is: we’ll show the burst meter so you understand what would happen in production pricing.

[12:42] Sam Ortega: Can we set a cap so we don’t accidentally run up burst?

[12:45] Hyejin Park: Yes. We can set an admission control cap above the committed level, like “allow up to 1.5x for up to N minutes,” and then clamp.

[12:55] Jordan Lee: That’s what we want. A predictable policy.

[12:58] Simran Kaur: Great. For Tier Plus we usually phrase it as “burst supported, not guaranteed,” but we can operationalize it with caps. We’ll propose a default burst ceiling for the POC.

[13:12] Priya Nair: When you clamp, is it a hard throttle or queue?

[13:16] Hyejin Park: Typically we first queue within bounds, then shed with a 429 or 503 depending. We can choose the behavior—some teams prefer 429 to signal client-side backoff.

[13:29] Sam Ortega: 429 is better for us.

[13:31] Jordan Lee: Yeah.

[13:33] Simran Kaur: Okay. We’ll set overload response to 429 with retry-after.

[13:38] Stephanie Nguyen: I want to make sure we capture success criteria in a measurable way. Can I propose we draft a table and you edit it?

[13:45] Jordan Lee: Yes.

[13:46] Stephanie Nguyen: Example entries: “During a 30-minute sustained load test at agreed traffic mix, deployment maintains >= X total tokens/sec and p95 TTFT <= 2.5s for common-case prompts.” And “During a 10-minute burst at 1.5x traffic, system accepts at least Y% of requests and maintains p95 under some threshold.”

[14:08] Jordan Lee: That’s good. But the big one is the floor. The number has to be credible.

[14:13] Simran Kaur: We’ll derive X from benchmarking your prompts on the proposed shape. We don’t want to guess.

[14:20] Priya Nair: Will you run the bench with our exact prompts? We can share anonymized.

[14:24] Simran Kaur: Yes, anonymized is fine. Even better if you can include approximate token counts. We’ll run a harness with streaming enabled.

[14:35] Sam Ortega: And concurrency. Don’t just do single stream.

[14:38] Simran Kaur: Absolutely. We’ll test with a concurrency profile. We’ll share the harness parameters.

[14:44] Jordan Lee: Okay.

[14:46] Stephanie Nguyen: Any security constraints for POC? Like logging retention, PII.

[14:51] Jordan Lee: We can use synthetic prompts for POC. For production we’ll need tighter controls.

[14:57] Priya Nair: We do want to know if prompts are stored.

[15:00] Stephanie Nguyen: For Dedicated, prompts are not used for training. Logs retention is configurable; we can turn down or off request/response logging. Metrics are aggregated.

[15:12] Sam Ortega: Can we still get debug if logging is off?

[15:15] Hyejin Park: We can do sampled logging or “headers only” logging to debug without payload.

[15:21] Jordan Lee: That’s fine.

[15:24] (crosstalk)
[15:24] Priya Nair: Sorry—
[15:25] Sam Ortega: Yeah—
[15:26] Priya Nair: For the throughput SLO, do you exclude warmup? Like initial deploy.

[15:31] Simran Kaur: Yes, there’s a warm pool behavior. During deploy or scaling events there can be warmup time. For SLO measurement, there’s typically an exclusion for the first X minutes after a rollout, and we recommend pinning and not rolling during your load test.

[15:49] Jordan Lee: For POC, we can keep it stable.

[15:52] Stephanie Nguyen: Great.

[15:54] Simran Kaur: Another edge case: if your client cancels streaming early, tokens/sec changes. We’ll measure what we generate, not what you would have generated. So in POC, use a harness that consumes the full output.

[16:09] Sam Ortega: Good call.

[16:11] Priya Nair: We can do that.

[16:13] Stephanie Nguyen: So, to recap where we are: BluePeak wants Tier Plus, with a pinned model/version for POC. We’ll propose an A100 shape in us-west unless H100 is available. Success criteria will cover throughput floor, latency, burst behavior, and observability exports.

[16:32] Jordan Lee: Yep.

[16:34] Stephanie Nguyen: What about support expectations during POC? Tier Plus includes faster response targets in production, but for POC we can set a Slack channel and an oncall window.

[16:44] Sam Ortega: We’d like a shared Slack. Our team will be testing at odd hours.

[16:48] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay, we can do a shared Connect channel.

[16:52] Hyejin Park: And we can set a maintenance window so we don’t do changes during your tests.

[16:57] Jordan Lee: Great.

[17:00] (brief pause)

[17:02] Priya Nair: One more question. If we exceed context length—like 20k—does it just error?

[17:07] Simran Kaur: Depends on the model and config. Some shapes support larger context, but throughput is different. For POC, we’ll set a max context for the acceptance test. For long context, we can test it separately and provide observed throughput.

[17:23] Priya Nair: Okay, that works.

[17:25] Jordan Lee: And later we might need multi-model. But again, not for this POC.

[17:30] Stephanie Nguyen: Right. Dedicated SLOs are per deployment; multi-model gets tricky, but we can discuss later.

[17:38] Maya Chen: Hi, sorry I’m late—Maya from procurement ops. Quick question, for this pilot is there a standard pilot agreement or is it under our MSA?

[17:48] Stephanie Nguyen: Hi Maya. Usually pilot can be under a short order form or a pilot addendum. We’ll send the commercial structure after we confirm scope and shape availability.

[18:00] Maya Chen: Okay. And you mentioned service credits in the real agreement—just want to know if that’s standard.

[18:06] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes, standard for enterprise Dedicated terms. For the pilot, it’s generally “best efforts” but we’ll use the success criteria.

[18:16] Maya Chen: Got it.

[18:18] Sam Ortega: On reporting, can we get an export that we can hand to finance—like “committed vs burst usage”?

[18:26] Stephanie Nguyen: Yes. That’s actually part of why we’re formalizing tiering. We can provide a usage export that separates committed throughput usage and burst consumption. For POC, we can provide a sample report.

[18:41] Jordan Lee: Perfect.

[18:43] Simran Kaur: Let’s talk about the actual POC steps. Typically: Week 0 kickoff + access, Week 1 baseline test, Week 2 burst test + tuning, Week 3 run in shadow or limited prod.

[18:57] Jordan Lee: We can do that. We’d like some real traffic, maybe 5%.

[19:02] Priya Nair: We can route a subset.

[19:05] Hyejin Park: We can set up a dedicated endpoint and you can route by header or by environment.

[19:12] Sam Ortega: We’ll need to monitor error rates closely.

[19:15] Simran Kaur: Yep. We’ll include error budget style reporting. But again, for POC it’s simpler: keep error rate below X% excluding client cancels.

[19:27] Jordan Lee: Okay.

[19:29] Stephanie Nguyen: Any final concerns?

[19:32] Jordan Lee: Just don’t overpromise on burst. We’ve had vendors say “burst unlimited” and then it’s like, no.

[19:39] Stephanie Nguyen: Totally. Our positioning is: floor is committed; burst is opportunistic with policy controls. We’ll write it clearly.

[19:48] Priya Nair: And provide the dashboard access day one.

[19:51] Simran Kaur: Yes.

[19:52] Stephanie Nguyen: Cool. We’ll send: (1) POC plan + success criteria table, (2) proposed shape options in us-west with lead time, (3) what data we need from you—prompts + token stats.

[20:07] Jordan Lee: Sounds good.

[20:09] Stephanie Nguyen: Thanks all. We’ll follow up tomorrow.

[20:12] (meeting continues with light scheduling / calendar holds; transcript truncated due to end-of-call cleanup)

[48:41] Stephanie Nguyen: Okay, I’ll drop a calendar hold for kickoff early next week.
[48:45] Jordan Lee: Great.
[48:46] Priya Nair: Thanks.
[48:47] Sam Ortega: Thanks.
[48:49] Hyejin Park: Thank you.
[48:50] Simran Kaur: Thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
